posts.caption: I walked into the feed room at six this morning and found the door standing open, which is usually my first sign that I did it myself. I had set the latch carefully. I had even given it a little tug the way you do. Pudding was sitting in the aisle looking like a man who had just finished a very honest day of work. There was grain on the floor in a neat trail leading straight to him. I swept it up while he supervised. Then I checked the latch again, and it was fine.
posts.first: Our first feed room had a screen door and a hook, and the pony before Pudding learned the hook in an afternoon. I spent that whole winter adding locks. The pony spent it patiently working through them one at a time. I've stopped counting the locks and started counting the days between incidents. We are at two.

posts.caption: There was a tense moment at the kitchen table last week involving a spreadsheet. My husband had printed it. He had highlighted things. I looked at the column labeled hay and I looked at the column labeled everything else, and I decided to bring up the boat that has been sitting behind the garage since 2019. It has not touched water in six years. We both looked out the window at Big Red, who was looking back in at us. He closed the folder. I put the kettle on.
posts.first: I keep the receipts for the horse in a coffee can in the tack room, and he keeps the receipts for the boat in a drawer in the garage. Neither of us has ever opened the other one. It's the longest running agreement we have. I think that's what people mean when they talk about a strong marriage.

posts.quote: The new mounting block has been in the arena for two weeks. The horses inspect it daily and have yet to reach a verdict.
posts.first: I carried the mounting block out to the arena myself and set it by the rail. Pudding walked a full circle around it before he would look at me. The Old Timer lined up beside it and went to sleep. The Diva has asked to see the paperwork. I'm told a decision is expected by spring.

posts.caption: The first hard freeze came in on a Tuesday, and I was out at five with the kettle, a hammer, and a bucket of hot water like I do every year. By the second morning my hands had given up. So the next payday I ordered the heated bucket and told everyone it was for efficiency. It arrived in a box the size of a small refrigerator. I spent a Saturday running the cord safely along the wall, and checked it three times before bed. The Homebody drank from it like it had always been there.
posts.first: My mother kept a pot of water on the back burner all winter for the barn cats, and never said a word about it. I thought it was just a habit of hers. Now I check the bucket before I brush my teeth. I understand her a little better every December.

posts.caption: The groomer came on Thursday to give everyone a quick trim before the cold set in, and I was in the house making coffee when I heard the clippers cut out mid-stroke. I walked out to find a very long silence and a patch along the Diva's neck that looked like a typo. She held her head high all the way back to her stall. For two days she would only be photographed from the left. I have decided to say it's called a lived-in look.
posts.first: I once dyed my own hair at the kitchen sink the night before a family wedding, and it came out a color the box had not promised. I wore it anyway, chin up, all weekend. Nobody mentioned it to my face. I recognized that walk when the Diva came out of the barn on Thursday.

posts.caption: We get a lot of drive-by visitors this time of year, mostly people who want to see the leaves and end up at our fence. A woman came up the lane Sunday with a thermos and a very sincere interest in how things work around here. The Old Timer let her talk for a good ten minutes. He doesn't move for anything but the feed truck. When she finally went back to her car, he turned and watched her leave with what I can only describe as professional satisfaction.
posts.first: The Old Timer came to us at twenty-two, retired from a lesson barn, and we didn't know what to do with him. We tried a schedule, a program, a little light work. He turned down all of it by standing there. Four years later it's still the best decision anyone on this farm has made.
